summary: The developer machine has everything needed to start building the Python LangChain order-history agent against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. Key developer tools (python, pip, node, docker), the documentdb MCP server (data-plane) and Microsoft Learn doc search are present, and numerous documentdb-* guidance skills are installed. Several model/embedding choices, a synthetic seed dataset, and one accelerator (DocumentDB Agent Kit) are missing and will require the builder's decisions or an install. Multiple cold answers in the prompt were confused with Azure Cosmos DB (RU/legacy) or with MongoDB; I verified the current facts and listed the exact corrections and sources.
summary_points: Build can start: python, pip, node, docker, the documentdb MCP server and the DocumentDB guidance skills are available and usable for code + verification.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated — most commonly confused with Azure Cosmos DB (request-unit model and *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com connection strings) or with upstream MongoDB; I verified the correct facts and provided authoritative Learn links.
Missing but useful accelerator: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — adds sample templates and agent patterns; its absence does not block the build but slows it.
Missing developer items worth adding: mongosh (helpful for manual verification). Other missing CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are not required for this sample and can be deprioritized.

Information gaps the builder must resolve before completing the sample: which LLM + embedding model to use, a concrete seed dataset and size, and whether tests must run without a live cluster (mocking requirements).

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the sample app, seed scripts, tests, install Python packages (pymongo, langchain, embeddings/LLM SDK).
tools.impact_if_missing: Sample cannot be built or executed locally.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install runtime dependencies (pymongo, langchain, OpenAI/Azure SDKs).
tools.detail: pip available via the Python install.
tools.workaround: Use a prebuilt environment/container that already contains required packages; but not recommended.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection, create/list collections and indexes, run explain/explain operations, aggregate and find for verification against the live cluster.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server available with 18 data-plane tools including documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_aggregate, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_explain_operation.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder couldn't inspect cluster state, create/verify indexes, sample documents or run explain plans programmatically; manual verification would be slower and error-prone.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh (if available) or the Azure portal to inspect the cluster; but automation and explain() calls would be missing.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Ground facts against official Microsoft docs to check recommendations, CLI names, API shapes, and examples.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent couldn't automatically verify product facts; higher risk of using out-of-date memory.
tools.workaround: Manual web searches or local doc copies; slower and less reliable.

tools.name: documentdb-* installed skills
tools.needed_for: Guidance during implementation: driver best-practices (documentdb-driver), connection tuning (documentdb-connection), local dev setup (documentdb-local-deployment), indexing & vector guidance (documentdb-indexing, documentdb-vector-search), deployment guidance (documentdb-azure-deployment) and natural-language query generation (documentdb-natural-language-querying).
tools.detail: Many domain skills are installed (documentdb-driver, documentdb-connection, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-natural-language-querying, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lose targeted, high-value implementation guidance; still possible to build using Learn docs and driver docs, but more error-prone and slower.
tools.workaround: Rely on Microsoft Learn pages and general MongoDB docs; reimplement best-practices ad-hoc.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Optional: inspect Azure resources, view cluster resource in portal, adjust firewall or private endpoint if needed for dev IP access; not required to build the sample against an existing cluster if connectivity is already available.
tools.detail: az CLI available (azure-cli 2.89.1). documentdb extension may be present in extensions list.
tools.impact_if_missing: Some control-plane operations (firewall updates) would require portal or REST calls instead.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal to change firewall or private endpoint settings; use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Installing MCP skills, running agent-kit installers, or Node-based verification scripts. Not required for Python sample itself, but helpful for agent-tooling and accelerators.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run npx-based skill installers; agent-kit install would be harder.
tools.workaround: Install skills manually or use Python-based templates.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optionally run the DocumentDB local Gateway container for offline development or tests; seed containers for integration tests.
tools.detail: Docker present; no local DocumentDB container running by default.
tools.impact_if_missing: No local container option for offline tests; must test against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test only against the live cluster (the run environment already specifies a reachable cluster).

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (install: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit)

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (i.e., resource type 'mongoClusters' under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer gave the Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts), which is the older Cosmos DB account resource shape used by Cosmos DB control-plane APIs and the Mongo API under Cosmos DB (RU-based). Azure DocumentDB (the vCore product) uses a dedicated resource type 'mongoClusters'.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC, they'd target the wrong resource model (Cosmos DB account) and fail to deploy or manage the intended Azure DocumentDB cluster; CLI commands and ARM templates wouldn't map to the new cluster resource 'mongoClusters'.
improvements: Update quickstarts and 'create cluster' examples to explicitly show 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' and the CLI group (az documentdb mongocluster) instead of older 'databaseAccounts' examples.
Add a deprecation note on older 'databaseAccounts' pages clarifying that 'mongoClusters' is the correct resource type for the vCore product and link to the new ARM template docs.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: az cosmosdb (core CLI group). Example: az cosmosdb create -g MyRG -n my-docdb-account --kind MongoDB
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct CLI group for Azure DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (part of the documentdb extension commands). Example commands: az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show / az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI reference)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the Azure Cosmos DB (account/resourceAccounts) CLI pattern (az cosmosdb) used for Cosmos DB accounts. Azure DocumentDB uses a distinct az documentdb command group for 'mongocluster' operations.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB - Connect a MongoDB application (cosmos mongodb connection docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands would target Cosmos DB resources or require different parameters; the builder would be unable to create or manage the intended 'mongoClusters' resources and might apply incorrect settings.
improvements: Document the CLI group 'az documentdb mongocluster' prominently on quickstarts and the top-level 'Get started' pages for Azure DocumentDB.
Add a single-line mapping in the agent kit README: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) -> az documentdb mongocluster'.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts'. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource type name 'azurerm_cosmosdb_account').
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM: use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (ARM/Bicep template path: microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters). Terraform: use the AzAPI / microsoft.documentdb/mongoClusters resource (examples on Microsoft Learn and Azure Verified Modules reference the mongoClusters resource or AzAPI provider modules for vCore 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep / templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer referenced the older Cosmos DB account resource and azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform resource, which were used for Cosmos DB (including the Mongo API RU-based accounts). The vCore product uses a dedicated 'mongoClusters' resource family.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used azurerm_cosmosdb_account or Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC, it would not create the Azure DocumentDB vCore cluster and the provisioning or subsequent configuration would fail or target the wrong product.
improvements: Update IaC quickstarts and sample repos to show a Bicep snippet using Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and include a Terraform AzAPI example that targets the mongoClusters resource.
Add an agent-kit rule that selects the right ARM/Terraform resource type based on the sample's stated target (Azure DocumentDB vs Cosmos DB).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer:
Use standard MongoDB URIs. Example (SRV): mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false
Or non-SRV: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings use mongodb+srv:// scheme to a host under the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com domain; cluster nodes listen starting at port 10260 for direct endpoints (query-from-any-node uses ports 10260+). TLS must be enabled (tls=true/tls parameter), recommended authMechanism is SCRAM-SHA-256 for native auth or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra identities, and recommended driver options include retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS settings. (Do NOT use the old *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern — that's Cosmos DB for MongoDB.)

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID: Get cluster credentials
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports and SRV)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the legacy Cosmos DB for MongoDB URI pattern (host suffix .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255). Azure DocumentDB uses a different host suffix (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and different node ports (starting 10260) and offers differing recommended authMechanism options.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB (cosmos mongo connection strings, port 10255)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the cosmos-style connection string (mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) the driver may fail to connect or connect to the wrong service type; using wrong host/port or wrong auth mechanism will cause connection failures and incorrect assumptions about supported features.
improvements: Add a 'Connection string quick mapping' section in the agent kit README that shows the three common Mongo URI families and which product they map to (Azure DocumentDB vCore: *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com, ports 10260+; Cosmos DB for MongoDB: *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com port 10255; MongoDB Atlas/self-hosted: normal hostnames/27017).
On the DocumentDB quickstarts page, explicitly call out the difference from Azure Cosmos DB's older connection examples.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Billed in Request Units (RUs) for Azure Cosmos DB accounts: you provision RU/s (fixed or autoscale) at the account/database/collection level. Cosmos DB also has a serverless option for some APIs; there is not a vCore-based pricing model for the MongoDB-compatible Cosmos API (billing is RU-based).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore product) is billed by compute tier (cluster tiers such as M30, M40 etc. that map to vCores and memory) and storage; there are no RUs. The pricing model is compute (vCores) + storage (and optional HA/replica costs), not RU-based Cosmos billing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (FAQ)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the RU-based Cosmos DB billing model (used by Cosmos DB accounts and the Cosmos Mongo API). Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses vCore-based cluster tiers and separate storage charges.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB pricing (RU model) and connection examples (confusing with Cosmos)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU-based throttling or planned the sample around RUs (e.g., setting RU budgets or autoscale), the produced sample would be misleading and tests for performance/cost would be wrong.
improvements: Add an explicit 'billing model' sentence at the top of DocumentDB quickstarts: 'Azure DocumentDB is billed by compute tier (vCores) + storage; it is NOT the RU-based Cosmos DB model.'
Add a short compare box on the DocumentDB vs Cosmos DB pages highlighting billing differences.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you authenticate with MongoDB credentials (SCRAM username/password) derived from Cosmos DB account keys or created MongoDB users. Typical auth is SCRAM-SHA with username/password encoded in the Mongo URI. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based auth is not generally available for the MongoDB-compatible API (AAD integration exists for other Cosmos APIs but not the Mongo wire protocol).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication for Mongo clients. Drivers can use MONGODB-OIDC / the MONGODB-OIDC connection string pattern (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC&authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:...). The cluster also exposes configuration flags (authAllowedModes) to allow NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (how-to-connect-role-based-access-control)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the older Cosmos Mongo API limitations (no AAD for data plane) and missed DocumentDB's explicit support for Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) as an authentication mode.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB API for MongoDB auth docs (older pages implying limited AAD support)

confusions.build_risk: Relying on username/password only could block implementations that intend to demonstrate role-based access using managed identities or OIDC; the sample might mis-document supported authentication patterns.
improvements: Add an explicit example in the agent kit for building connection strings using Microsoft Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC) and an example for native SCRAM-SHA-256 usage, with a note about required cluster preview settings.
In the 'how to connect' quickstart, provide a one-line code snippet for constructing the MONGODB-OIDC URI in at least one language.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python: pymongo). There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK for data-plane Mongo operations — the azure-cosmos SDK is for the SQL/Core API, not the Mongo wire-protocol API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo for Python). There is no separate service-specific data-plane SDK for Mongo operations; azure-cosmos SDK targets the SQL/Core API, so the app should use the MongoDB driver.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility)

confusions.build_risk: None — this is correct.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: I do not believe the Cosmos DB MongoDB API exposes MongoDB-native vector indexes in the same way as a native MongoDB 7+ cluster. Historically Cosmos has not provided native MongoDB vector-index DDL; therefore there is no standard db.collection.createIndex(...) vector index command on Cosmos Mongo API that I would rely on.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes an integrated vector store and supports multiple vector index kinds (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann). You create them via the createIndexes/createIndex style templates with a 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' object or by using createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-ivf' | 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-diskann' and options like dimensions, similarity, numLists / lBuild / maxDegree. Use $search and the 'cosmosSearch' operator in aggregation pipelines to query vectors.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search overview and examples)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF/DiskANN examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed Cosmos DB's older lack of vector-index DDL or conflated the older Cosmos Mongo API capabilities with Azure DocumentDB's integrated vector search features. The modern Azure DocumentDB vCore product explicitly includes vector indexes (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB historically recommended Azure Cognitive Search for text & vector (older pattern)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder believed vector indexing wasn't available, they'd skip adding an integrated vector index and either attempt an external vector store or provide a misleading sample. For LangChain agent memory/semantic search demos, that would produce suboptimal code and unnecessary external dependencies.
improvements: Document the 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' vector-index creation pattern in quickstarts and in the agent kit, including typical parameter recommendations (dimensions, numLists, lBuild, lSearch).
Add one short vector-index example to the agent kit sample for Python (create index + run $search).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search connected to Cosmos DB as the indexer/source for full-text search. For hybrid (text + vector) search combine Azure Cognitive Search's semantic/vector features with fields indexed from Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB itself does not provide a built‑in full-text search engine for Mongo wire protocol; use Azure Search or an external engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an integrated full-text search engine (BM25) and integrated vector search; full-text search indexes are created with createSearchIndexes and queried using the $search aggregation stage (BM25). Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is supported on the same cluster and can be fused (e.g., Reciprocal Rank Fusion) inside an aggregation pipeline or via client-side fusion. You do not need Azure Cognitive Search for this functionality.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (overview and how it works)
Full-text search - BM25 keyword search (examples)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector fusion)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described an older integration pattern (Cosmos DB + Azure Cognitive Search) or assumed the product did not include a native search engine. Azure DocumentDB vCore now includes integrated BM25 full-text search and hybrid capabilities.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB integration docs (older recommended approach)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used external Azure Cognitive Search instead of the integrated search, the sample would be more complex, require extra provisioning, and not demonstrate DocumentDB's native capabilities; example queries would look different and results (scores, pipelines) would not match the product's $search semantics.
improvements: Update the product quickstarts to include a small 'full-text and hybrid search' example using createSearchIndexes and $search to make it discoverable for agents.
Include a dedicated example in the agent kit showing server-side RRF fusion with $unionWith, to reduce confusion about client-side vs server-side fusion options.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol that maps to specific Mongo versions; historically supported versions have included MongoDB 3.2, 3.6, 4.0 and later added 4.2/5.0 in some regions. It does not implement every MongoDB server feature — common omissions are server-side JavaScript ($where/$eval), some admin commands, and certain storage-engine specific features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (documented explicitly). The service implements the vast majority of MongoDB operators (99.03% coverage); administrative commands are managed by the platform and some special admin commands or certain features may be limited/absent. Builders should consult the 'MongoDB compatibility' operator list before relying on niche admin commands.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility and supported wire protocol versions)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer listed older or generic Cosmos/legacy Mongo API versions; DocumentDB explicitly documents support for modern wire protocol versions (5.0-8.0).

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API compatibility pages and older Mongo versions references

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used assumptions about supported server versions (e.g., thinking only 3.x was supported), they might limit the sample to older syntax or avoid modern aggregation stages that DocumentDB actually supports, reducing the sample's usefulness.
improvements: Call out supported wire-protocol versions (5.0-8.0) at the top of the 'Get started' or 'Overview' pages and add a short 'features not available' link to the compatibility reference so agents can quickly see unsupported admin commands.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Run a local MongoDB Docker image for MongoDB-protocol compatible development (e.g., docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:6.0). The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator exists but historically does not provide full MongoDB API parity; therefore use the official MongoDB image on port 27017 for local development and tests.
confusions.grounded_answer: The DocumentDB local Gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) is the recommended local runtime for development; it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Use the Gateway image and the local 'Gateway' docker-compose pattern. If the builder must test parity with the live cluster, use the DocumentDB Gateway container (port 10260) with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 settings to mirror production behaviour.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-local-deployment skill text (local Gateway image and port 10260)

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
Local Deployment & Developer Workflow — Azure DocumentDB (Gateway image and ports)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a generic MongoDB docker image on 27017 (common for self-hosted Mongo), whereas the DocumentDB project provides a Gateway image with different default ports and TLS/credential requirements.

confusion_sources.title: Official MongoDB Docker image docs (common 27017 pattern)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses a vanilla mongo:6.0 container for local integration tests, the local environment would not reflect DocumentDB-specific features (ports, TLS configuration, SCRAM behavior, vector search, search indexes), causing integration tests to pass locally but fail against the real cluster.
improvements: Make the 'local dev' gateway image and a minimal docker-compose example one of the top-level 'Get started' artifacts so agents reuse the same local image and port (10260).
In the agent kit, include a small docker-compose.yml snippet that binds 10260 and shows required env vars (SKIP_INIT_DATA, INIT_DATA_PATH).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: The Cosmos DB MongoDB API does not reliably support MongoDB change streams as implemented by upstream MongoDB. Instead use the Cosmos DB Change Feed (data-plane feature) which is enabled at the account/collection level; you must use the Change Feed APIs rather than MongoDB change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-compatible change streams (documentdb change streams). The service provides a change streams API with resume tokens and multi-shard support (with some preview details for multi-shard change streams). There is explicit documentation on how to open watch()/aggregate with $changeStream and guidance about resumability and limits.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (how-to and examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed Cosmos DB change feed semantics and older advice about change streams on Cosmos' Mongo API; Azure DocumentDB explicitly documents support for Mongo-style change streams with resume tokens and additional multi-shard features.

confusion_sources.title: Change feed in Azure Cosmos DB and change stream mapping for Cosmos API

confusions.build_risk: If the builder believed change streams were unsupported, they might implement a polling/lease-based workaround or omit a streaming demo, losing fidelity and correctness for an event-driven order-status watch feature.
improvements: Clarify the DocumentDB change-stream docs with a short 'Compare to Cosmos DB change feed' sidebar so agents don't conflate the two products.
Ensure the agent kit includes a small sample that opens a change stream and demonstrates resumeAfter to minimize confusion.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (the service-specific MCP server) for data-plane inspection and tooling against Cosmos DB / DocumentDB accounts. The general Azure MCP Server handles control-plane resource management but the documentdb MCP has Mongo/Cosmos-specific data-plane helpers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools for Azure DocumentDB (queries, index management, explain, createIndex, sampleDocuments); the general 'azure' server is for control-plane/management and best-practice lookups.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server present) and relevant docs describing data-plane tooling

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.build_risk: None — correct and the MCP server is available in the inventory.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally named its NoSQL offering DocumentDB; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB became the SQL API within Cosmos DB). This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB — they are not the same codebase.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a common source of confusion. Historically 'DocumentDB' was the name of Microsoft's earlier NoSQL offering that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The current 'Azure DocumentDB' vCore product is a distinct offering (with DocumentDB engine lineage) and is separate from 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)' and also separate from Amazon DocumentDB. The open-source DocumentDB engine (github.com/documentdb/documentdb) is the engine that powers the Azure DocumentDB product; Microsoft DocumentDB (old name) that became Cosmos DB is a different historical product. In short: (a) the name 'DocumentDB' is overloaded historically; (b) the new Azure DocumentDB product is a vCore MongoDB-compatible managed service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine, not the older Cosmos DB account resource model.

grounding_links.title: Frequently asked questions about Azure DocumentDB (FAQ) - relation to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes the historical name changes with present-day product lines. The old 'Azure DocumentDB' was rebranded as Cosmos DB, while the new 'Azure DocumentDB' (vCore) is a separate, modern product that shares an engine name with the open-source DocumentDB project.

confusion_sources.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ (explains relationship and history)

confusions.build_risk: Name confusion could cause the builder to use the wrong CLI commands, resource types, or docs, or to target Cosmos DB APIs instead of Azure DocumentDB vCore. Samples and READMEs might mislabel the product leading to developer confusion.
improvements: Add a single-line 'Terminology' banner at the top of the Azure DocumentDB docs clarifying: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is different from the older DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB; do not use Cosmos DB tutorials for this product.'
Add a quick 'Which product is this sample for?' checkbox in the agent kit templates so generated README text uses the correct product name.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB-compatible API there is Cosmos DB's proprietary engine that implements the Mongo wire protocol. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers and usual APIs, but expect behavioral differences (indexing, consistency, some unsupported commands, RU-based throughput) — thoroughly test queries and features you rely on.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB project) rather than MongoDB's server code; it implements the MongoDB wire protocol to present a MongoDB-compatible API. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) and APIs, but test for the small set of differences; however, the runtime engine is DocumentDB (open-source) not Cosmos DB's older engine. Billing and scaling behave according to the vCore model.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (notes on engine and compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a proprietary Cosmos engine; the correct fact is that Azure DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine and implements the Mongo wire protocol. The practical guidance (use Mongo drivers and test for differences) remains valid but the engine attribution was incorrect.

confusion_sources.title: Azure DocumentDB overview and engine notes

confusions.build_risk: Incorrect statements about the engine could mislead developers about portability and licensing concerns; however, application-level code (drivers, queries) should still be written against the MongoDB wire protocol and tested, so practical build risk is low.
improvements: Add a small 'Engine & compatibility' note on quickstarts clarifying 'DocumentDB engine (open-source) powers Azure DocumentDB; you still use Mongo drivers, but check compatibility docs for edge cases.'

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named 'sample_retail_06' for everything the sample creates and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the prompt explicitly instructs to use database 'sample_retail_06'.

confusions.question: How should the sample read the cluster connection string at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (e.g., in Python: uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Never hard-code the secret.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run-environment states the connection string is in DOCUMENTDB_URI and must be read at runtime and not committed.

confusions.question: What indexes will the sample create for order-history queries?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a time-series friendly index to support timeline and aggregation queries: db.orders.createIndex({ customer_id: 1, order_date: -1 }) and a unique index on order_id: db.orders.createIndex({ order_id: 1 }, { unique: true }).
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a reasonable and recommended index shape for order-history queries: a compound index on { customer_id: 1, order_date: -1 } to support timeline queries (sorted by date per customer) and a unique index on order_id. The documentdb-indexing guidance supports these choices for read-heavy timeline queries.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-indexing skill guidance and Learn indexing docs

confusions.build_risk: None; creator should also add indexes required for aggregation pipelines used in spend summaries (e.g., index on order_date and customer_id if aggregation filters by date ranges).

confusions.question: How will the sample connect from Python using a Mongo driver?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo.MongoClient with the DOCUMENTDB_URI and TLS enabled. Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True); db = client['sample_retail_06']; orders = db['orders']
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard pymongo.MongoClient with the DOCUMENTDB_URI, enable TLS, and select the sample_retail_06 database. The documentdb-driver skill recommends a singleton MongoClient and connection reuse.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-driver skill and Learn docs on connecting with pymongo

confusions.question: Which client libraries will the sample use for the agent and memory?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo for data access and LangChain for the agent and memory (e.g., langchain.memory.ConversationBufferMemory). Install packages: pip install pymongo langchain.
confusions.grounded_answer: Reasonable default: use pymongo for data access and LangChain for agent logic and memory. The project must still decide the LLM provider and the embedding model; LangChain integrates with many providers. The documentdb skills and LangChain docs are the correct references.

information_gaps.title: LLM and embedding model selection
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or doc defines which LLM and embedding provider/models the sample should use (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, local models). This affects embedding dimensions, which vector index configuration to pick, and code examples (client init and environment variables). I looked for a default in the prompt, the installed skills, and the Learn docs and found none.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset and size / source
information_gaps.description: No skill or doc supplies the sample's seed data or where to get it. The prompt asks to 'load the sample data' but doesn't supply schema fields beyond implied ones. I searched installed skills and Learn docs for a sample_retail_06 seed and found none; the builder must author a seed script and decide record counts and sample shape.

information_gaps.title: Unit-test strategy for offline runs
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't say whether unit tests must run without a live cluster (mocking) or may run against the live cluster. The installed skills show how to run locally via the Gateway container, but do not define a CI strategy for mocking vs live-run tests. Decide whether tests should rely on the live cluster or include mock fixtures.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the documentdb resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' (CLI: az documentdb mongocluster) not 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' or az cosmosdb, which target the older Cosmos DB account model.

When you build connection URIs, use the Azure DocumentDB host format and ports: prefer mongodb+srv://<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com with TLS; direct node ports start at 10260. Do NOT reuse the older Cosmos DB for MongoDB host suffix and port 10255 pattern.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo) and a singleton MongoClient. For vector and full-text search use DocumentDB's integrated APIs: createSearchIndexes + $search for BM25, and create index with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) for vector search.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample. If you want to add automated app provisioning or template workflows, install Azure Developer CLI (`azd`) via its official installer; otherwise document controlling via Azure portal or az CLI is sufficient.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is not required to build this sample (cluster already exists). If the team wants to include IaC samples, install Bicep to author Bicep templates; otherwise use ARM/AzAPI snippets from Learn.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is not required for the sample because the run-environment already provides a cluster. Add Terraform only if you plan to supply a Terraform module for the sample; otherwise the builder can use ARM/Bicep examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: dotnet not required for a Python LangChain sample. Add only if you plan to produce a .NET variant of the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for interactive connectivity, manual checks of indexes, and running sample aggregation and $search queries by hand. Install via the official MongoDB installation instructions (e.g., apt / brew / MSI), or use the MongoDB Shell download from MongoDB.
